title: Election Day storm could impact voter turnout in key midterm states | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

A soggy storm will track through the central United States on Election Day and could influence voter turnout forkey races in the region.

Rain will fall on a widespread area from the Great Lakes, Plains and Upper Midwest to the western Gulf Coast Tuesday. Wet conditions are possible for key races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and eastern Texas.

The threat of flash flooding is low, but voters traveling to the polls could encounter ponding on roads.

Thunderstorms are expected on the storm’s southern side, a few of which could intensify and turn severe from eastern Texas to Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi. Damaging wind gusts will likely be the main threat from any severe storms.

Breezy conditions are also likely throughout a large portion of the central US, especially in the Plains. Kansas could see gusts between 30 to 40 mph.

The conditions will be a turnout factor in those states and for others in the central US who aren’t among the more than43 million people who have already cast ballotsthrough early voting.

Rainfall and other active weather tend to suppress voter turnout while sunshine has the opposite effect,multiplestudieshavefound.

Dry weather will likely bookend the storm along much of the East Coast and in the West. The only exception is coastal areas of the Southeast where nuisance showers can’t be completely ruled out yet.

There will be no need to bundle up. High temperatures in most of the nation’s eastern half are forecast to be 5 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit above average. Only the Southwest will have temperatures tilting a bit cooler than average.

The breakdown below shows the forecast for some of the key states in the midterms. Keep in mind these forecasts will likely change as confidence grows in the storm’s path by this weekend.
